title: Congress Leaves Without a Funding Deal as Trump's Clout Faces a Test
shortdescription: Congress heads home with no deal to avoid a December 11 shutdown, Republicans debate how much sway Trump will keep once Democrats take over, Nvidia's Huang is called to testify, and the Supreme Court takes up asylum.

sub.title: Washington pauses for Thanksgiving with a lot unfinished
sub.descr: Congress has left town for the holiday with a to-do list that is getting shorter on time and longer on problems. There is still no plan to keep the government funded past December 11, Republicans are talking openly about how much influence President Trump will have once Democrats take over in January, and a decision by Nvidia has pulled the White House into a fresh political argument. The Supreme Court has also agreed to hear a major immigration case. Here is a plain-English guide to the latest US political news.

sub.title: No Deal Yet to Avoid a December 11 Shutdown
sub.descr: Federal funding runs out at 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Friday, December 11. The House finished its votes for the week on November 20 and the Senate left for the holiday, with no stopgap bill text released in either chamber, leaving about eight legislative days before the deadline. Not one of the 12 funding bills for the current fiscal year, which began on October 1, has become law. The House has passed three of its 12 bills and the Senate none. The administration is reportedly considering a stopgap that runs through March, and House Appropriations Chair Tom Cole has floated pairing bipartisan bills with a short-term patch for everything else. Republican Rep. Mike Simpson said, "We're going to have to pass a (continuing resolution)." Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro wants any stopgap kept as short as possible, and several Senate Democrats say they will oppose a deal without language restricting war funding for Iran. Republicans need at least seven Senate Democrats to reach 60 votes.

sub.title: How Much Power Will Trump Keep After the Midterms?
sub.descr: On Tuesday, Trump pardoned two turkeys, Freedom and Feathers, at the White House, with Speaker Mike Johnson in attendance. Johnson loses the gavel in January, when Roll Call reports that Democrats will take control of the new Congress, which is seated on January 3. Republican senators were asked what that means for the president. Sen. James Lankford said Trump's influence will be "policy-to-policy," pointing out that he still has his veto pen and can direct agencies. Sen. Ted Cruz said it will "obviously, be different," and predicted Democrats will focus on attacking the president, but added that "the president will continue to lead." Trump said he would work with Democrats: "If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too."

sub.title: Huang's Return Draws a Political Response
sub.descr: Nvidia's decision on Monday to bring back CEO Jensen Huang spilled into Washington. Trump said he had been "speaking to the board directly and indirectly" before the move, and Nvidia said its board received input from senior US government levels and found no national security risk. Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan called the reinstatement a mistake, and Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine said it raised concerns about Trump's China policy. Roll Call reports that Huang is scheduled to appear before several congressional committees next week. Separately, Republican Sen. Jim Banks has questioned the administration's handling of air traffic control upgrades and its request for $50 billion in new funding.

sub.title: Supreme Court Agrees to Hear the Asylum Case
sub.descr: On Friday, November 13, the Supreme Court agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend asylum access for migrants at the US-Mexico border, in the case Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services. The justices will review a January 2025 proclamation and related Department of Homeland Security guidance. A federal judge and a D.C. Circuit panel largely ruled against the administration, though the restrictions remain in effect while it appeals. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called suspending illegal entry and asylum access among "the most important and effective pieces of the President's response." The challengers say the president cannot "invent by fiat a new removal system." Arguments are likely next spring, with no date set.

sub.title: What to Watch Next
sub.descr: Keep an eye on three things. First, whether congressional leaders agree on the length of a stopgap bill before December 11, and whether Iran war language blocks it in the Senate. Second, next week's congressional hearings with Jensen Huang. Third, how Trump handles his relationship with Democrats before the new Congress arrives on January 3. Check the latest updates before you publish.

title: Trump's Mixed Message on Immigration, a Food Tariff Fight and a December Funding Deadline
shortdescription: Trump hints at a softer immigration stance but names Stephen Miller chief of staff, Gov. Whitmer takes on food tariffs, and Congress faces a December 11 shutdown deadline.

sub.title: Washington is sending mixed signals after the midterms
sub.descr: Democrats are heading into the new Congress with real power, and it's already changing how Washington talks and acts. In just the last few days, President Donald Trump has hinted at a softer approach on immigration while quietly putting one of its hardest-line architects in charge of his staff. A governor has gone straight to the Treasury Department over grocery prices. The Supreme Court has pushed back on an attempt to change how ballots are counted. And Congress is staring at a funding deadline just a few weeks away. If you're trying to keep track of the latest US political news, here's a plain-English look at what's really going on.

sub.title: Trump Talks About a Softer Immigration Approach, Then Puts Stephen Miller in Charge
sub.descr: The biggest head-scratcher of the week came on immigration. After Democrats won control of the next Congress, Trump said his crackdown may have been "too tough" and told CBS's "60 Minutes": "I'd love to do something on immigration." Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff. It's hard to read those two moves together. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has made his own position clear, writing that "deportations will continue." On the ground, arrests are still being reported in California, Michigan, Massachusetts, Florida and Alabama, and immigration advocates in Miami say the arrests "have not ceased at all." So is this a real change of direction or just a change of tone? For now, who Trump puts in the room says more than what he says on camera.

sub.title: Gov. Whitmer Asks the Treasury to End Food Tariffs
sub.descr: Grocery bills have turned into a political fight of their own. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer sent a letter on Tuesday to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent asking the administration to end the food tariffs imposed in 2025 and 2026 and to reimburse Michigan residents for the higher costs. She pointed to figures from the National Taxpayers Union Foundation showing that Michigan households have faced an average tariff burden of $6,485 each since January 2025, which her office says is the highest in the country. She also noted that exports to Canada fell 12.3% last year. The Treasury Department didn't answer the letter directly. A spokesperson instead pointed to Bessent's recent comments that "food is below the Fed's targets" and that rising energy prices are an "energy shock" linked to the Iran conflict. It's a kitchen-table argument, and it's one that voters in both parties are likely to keep hearing about.

sub.title: Congress Faces a December 11 Shutdown Deadline
sub.descr: Back on Capitol Hill, lawmakers are returning to a long and messy to-do list. The most urgent item is funding the government. A stopgap bill has kept programs running since October 1, and Congress needs to pass another measure by December 11 to avoid a shutdown. Full-year spending bills worth about $1.9 trillion are unlikely to be finished in time, so most people expect another short-term patch that pushes the fight into 2027. There's plenty more waiting. The long-overdue farm bill needs Democratic votes and has become a fight over food aid, E15 fuel and conservation money. A final deal on the annual defense bill is possible. The House still has to decide whether to take up a Senate-passed college sports bill and a bipartisan permitting reform bill, and Senate Republicans want to confirm judges and other nominees before they leave for the holidays.

sub.title: Democrats Start Using Their New Leverage on Drug Prices
sub.descr: Even before they officially take over, Democrats are already flexing their new muscle. Incoming committee leaders have sent letters to all 27 drugmakers that signed "most favored nation" pricing agreements with the Trump administration, asking them to hand over the details of those deals, including unredacted contracts. The agreements tie Medicaid drug prices to the lower prices paid in other wealthy countries, and the White House has pitched them as a big win for patients. Democrats want to know if they truly deliver what was promised. It's a preview of how oversight is about to change. When the new Congress arrives in January, expect more letters, more hearings and tougher questions about whether the administration's health policies live up to the headlines.

sub.title: Courts Say Election Rules Can't Be Rewritten on the Fly
sub.descr: The courts have been just as busy. On November 2, the Supreme Court turned down an emergency request from the Trump administration that would have forced California to set aside ballots from about 20,000 voters suspected of being noncitizens. The order was short and came without any explanation or publicly noted dissent, so California can keep counting under its normal procedures. The next day, Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington temporarily barred federal officials from sending states lists of voters suspected of lacking citizenship and from pressuring election officials to separate ballots, citing concerns that the government's information could be wrong. The legal fight isn't over, but the early message from the courts has been clear. Changes to how elections are run need a solid legal basis, not an emergency shortcut.

sub.title: What to Watch Next in US Politics
sub.descr: So where does all of this leave us? Keep an eye on three things. First, whether Trump's immigration comments turn into actual policy, or whether the Miller appointment signals the crackdown is here to stay. Second, how Congress handles the December 11 deadline and whether Democrats and Republicans can cut a deal on the farm bill and the defense bill before the year ends. Third, how quickly Democrats move from letters to formal investigations once they take control in January. With prices still a major worry for households, expect the cost of living to stay at the center of nearly every political argument in the weeks ahead.

title: Tennessee GOP Pushes Memphis Redistricting for House Control
shortdescription: Tennessee GOP pushes Memphis redistricting as Trump-backed Republicans seek stronger House control by carving up the district.

sub.title: Late-Night Hearings and Public Outcry Over Memphis Map
sub.descr:
Tennessee’s Republican-led legislature is barreling toward a final vote Thursday on a controversial new U.S. House map that would effectively split up the majority-Black city of Memphis across multiple districts. The move, which has drawn sharp condemnation from civil rights groups and Democrats, is widely seen as an effort to unseat the state’s lone Democratic representative and give the GOP a better shot at protecting its slim House majority in November’s midterm elections.

During often-heated legislative hearings on Wednesday, protesters repeatedly interrupted proceedings, chanting and holding signs that read “Protect Our Vote” and “Hands Off Memphis.” Despite the disruption, Republican committee members pushed the redistricting bills forward, setting the stage for what is expected to be a party-line vote in both the full House and Senate as early as Thursday afternoon.

The proposed map carves up the current 9th Congressional District, which has long been anchored by Memphis and its majority-Black population. Under the new lines, Black voters would be scattered into three surrounding districts that lean heavily Republican, effectively diluting their political power. GOP leaders argue the changes are based on population shifts and political considerations — not race — but critics say the pattern is impossible to ignore.

sub.title: Playing Catch-Up With a Supreme Court Ruling
sub.descr:
The timing of Tennessee’s redistricting push is no accident. Republican strategists in multiple Southern states are moving quickly to take advantage of a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision that weakened a key provision of the Voting Rights Act. The court ruled that Louisiana had relied too heavily on race when it created a second majority-Black House district, upending decades of legal precedent that had protected such districts from being dismantled.

That ruling opened the door for states like Tennessee, Alabama, and South Carolina to redraw maps in the middle of the decade — something that was once considered legally risky. Tennessee’s current map was only upheld by the state Supreme Court in April 2022, which rejected a challenge at the time because the election was too close. But with the high court’s new guidance, Republicans feel emboldened to try again.

“This is Black vote dilution at an industrial scale,” said Sekou Franklin, a political science professor at Middle Tennessee State University who works with the Tennessee branch of the NAACP. Franklin and other activists argue that the GOP is using the Supreme Court’s ruling as a political weapon, not a legal necessity. Democrats have also pointed out that the August 6 primary is now less than three months away, warning that changing district lines this late will cause chaos for both candidates and voters trying to figure out where they can cast ballots.

sub.title: A Broader Southern Strategy to Flip Seats
sub.descr:
Tennessee isn’t acting alone. Across the South, Republican lawmakers are racing to lock in new congressional maps before the November midterms. In Alabama, the state House has already passed legislation that would trigger special congressional primaries if courts allow the state to set aside a federal court-ordered map that created a second district with a near-majority of Black voters. That map helped elect Democrat Shomari Figures in 2024, and Republicans want to erase that gain.

During a fiery four-hour debate in Alabama’s House, Democratic Representative Juandalynn Givan compared the GOP’s effort to the poll taxes and literacy tests of the Jim Crow era — specifically calling out a grotesque practice where Black voters were forced to guess the number of jelly beans in a jar to register. “It is a calculated political maneuver born out of fear,” Givan said. “A fear of Black people and, most importantly, Black political power.”

Meanwhile, South Carolina’s Republican-led Senate is expected to take up a resolution Thursday that would allow lawmakers to return after their regular session ends specifically to redraw congressional districts. That state’s only Democratic-held seat is squarely in the GOP’s crosshairs. Democratic Representative Justin Bamberg told his Republican colleagues during debate that he actually felt sorry for them, saying they were abandoning their principles just to follow the whims of former President Trump.

“The president of the United States is a very powerful man,” Bamberg said. “Wields a heavy, heavy thumb — Truth Social, X, Meta, Instagram. To be honest, I don’t envy our Republican colleagues.”

sub.title: What Happens Next in Tennessee
sub.descr:
Assuming the Tennessee map passes the full legislature on Thursday — as most political observers expect — it will then head to Republican Governor Bill Lee’s desk. Lee has not publicly committed to signing the bill, but he has also not voiced any opposition, and the GOP holds a supermajority that could override a veto if necessary.

The package of bills does more than just redraw lines. It also repeals a state law that explicitly prohibited mid-decade redistricting, removing a legal barrier that might have been used to challenge the move in state court. Additionally, the legislation reopens the candidate qualifying window, giving new candidates a chance to enter the primary and allowing existing candidates to switch districts if the map changes where they live.

Democrats have vowed to sue, arguing that the map violates the Voting Rights Act even under the Supreme Court’s narrower interpretation. But with time running short before the August primary, any legal challenge faces an uphill battle to stop the map from being used this year. For now, civil rights groups are focused on public pressure, hoping that sustained protests and media attention might push a few Republican moderates to reconsider.

Whether that happens remains to be seen. But one thing is clear: Tennessee has become the latest battlefield in a national redistricting war that could determine control of Congress for the next two years, and the fight over Memphis is far from over.

title: Democrats Fight $1 Billion White House Security Plan
shortdescription: Senate Democrats oppose a $1 billion White House security funding plan tied to Trump’s ballroom project amid Republican division.

sub.title: A Partisan Budget Fight Over Ballroom Security
sub.descr:
A massive political clash is brewing on Capitol Hill as Democrats vow to dismantle a $1 billion Senate Republican security proposal that they argue is little more than a taxpayer-funded contribution to a lavish White House ballroom project backed by President Donald Trump.

As Republican lawmakers return to Washington after a recess, they are facing pointed questions about the hefty spending measure, which ties together funding for immigration enforcement and security upgrades for the East Wing of the White House – upgrades directly linked to a planned ballroom that Trump has championed for years. Democrats, led by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, say they will use every procedural tool at their disposal to kill the proposal or force Republicans into politically damaging votes.

The controversy centers on a spending bill that Senate Republicans are trying to push through using a partisan budget maneuver known as reconciliation, which would allow them to pass the legislation without a single Democratic vote. The bill originally aimed to restore funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other border agencies – funding that Democrats have blocked since February over policy disagreements related to deportations and detention standards. But in a surprise move, Republican negotiators added a massive $1 billion appropriation for White House security, officially designated for the U.S. Secret Service.

sub.title: Schumer Calls It a 'Billion-Dollar Ballroom' Giveaway
sub.descr:
In a letter sent to Democratic colleagues early Monday, Schumer did not mince words. He accused Republicans of exploiting a moment of national security concern to funnel billions into what he called a 'rogue ICE operation' and a 'billion-dollar ballroom' – all while ignoring working families crushed by rising costs and doing nothing to end U.S. military involvement in Iran.

'The Republican-controlled Congress is preparing to answer this moment with a deficit-busting, party-line bill that pours billions more taxpayer dollars into a rogue ICE operation and a billion-dollar ballroom,' Schumer wrote. He added that Democrats would fight the measure by pressing the Senate parliamentarian to strike the ballroom security money from the bill as a violation of budget rules, and by offering amendments that would force Republicans to publicly defend the spending.

Schumer's strategy is twofold: first, argue that the security money is non-germane to a spending bill focused on immigration enforcement, and second, make moderate Republicans in tough reelection races choose between party loyalty and fiscal conservatism. The bill's language specifies that the money would support enhancements to the ballroom project, 'including above-ground and below-ground security features,' but says it may not be used for non-security elements. Critics argue that distinction is meaningless when the entire project is designed to benefit Trump personally.

sub.title: Republican Skepticism Emerges on the Hill
sub.descr:
Despite Republican leaders' hopes to fast-track the bill, it is far from clear that the $1 billion security package has enough support within their own caucus. The House has not yet released its version of the spending legislation, but the Senate is expected to begin voting on its proposal later this week. During the recess, most GOP lawmakers avoided commenting on the ballroom provision, but a few have publicly signaled unease.

Rep. Rob Wittman, a Virginia Republican who briefly gaveled in a pro forma House session last week, told reporters he needs to see detailed breakdowns before making up his mind. 'I'm going to look at it very carefully and make sure those things are in the national interest,' Wittman said. 'I want to know the exact nature of the expenditures that would go there for security. So I think it's a little premature to look at that and say, you know, yes or no to it.'

Wittman emphasized that he wants to understand how the ballroom-related security costs fit into the overall construction budget and whether the Secret Service truly requested the full $1 billion. Other Republican members, speaking on condition of anonymity, have privately expressed concerns about the optics of funding a ballroom for Trump while constituents struggle with inflation and high interest rates.

sub.title: The Ballroom's Turbulent History and Legal Fights
sub.descr:
Trump has pushed for the East Wing ballroom project for years, arguing that the White House lacks a proper space for large official receptions and press events. After a man named Cole Tomas Allen was charged in April with storming the White House Correspondents' Association dinner at the Washington Hilton carrying guns and knives, Trump and Republican leaders seized on the incident to renew calls for hardened security around the executive mansion.

The White House has since filed court documents describing the proposed East Wing project as 'heavily fortified,' including bomb shelters, military command posts, and an underground medical facility. Trump himself has said the ballroom should feature bulletproof glass and defenses capable of repelling drone attacks. Trump has also claimed the ballroom's construction would cost $400 million and use private funds, but he had not previously proposed a specific number for security costs – making the Senate's $1 billion figure a surprise to many lawmakers.

However, the National Trust for Historic Preservation has filed a lawsuit to block construction, arguing the project would damage the historic character of the White House. A federal appeals court last month allowed construction to continue while the case proceeds. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle praised Republicans last week for including the security money, calling the project 'long overdue.' Ingle said the funds would 'provide the United States Secret Service with the resources they need to fully and completely harden the White House complex, in addition to the many other critical missions for the USSS.'

With Democrats preparing a procedural war and Republicans themselves divided, the fate of the $1 billion security proposal – and the ballroom it would protect – remains deeply uncertain. All eyes will be on the Senate floor this week as Schumer and his caucus try to strip the provision out, amendment by amendment, while the clock ticks toward a potential government funding deadline.

title: Andy Biggs Wins Arizona GOP Primary, Faces Katie Hobbs
shortdescription: Andy Biggs wins the Arizona GOP primary, setting up a governor race against Katie Hobbs in the 2026 election as both parties target this key battleground state.

sub.title: Biggs Secures Republican Nomination
sub.descr: Republican Rep. Andy Biggs has won the Arizona GOP gubernatorial primary, securing the party’s nomination for a high-profile November election contest against Democratic incumbent Gov. Katie Hobbs. Biggs, a longtime conservative and close ally of former President Donald Trump, defeated fellow Republican Rep. David Schweikart and other challengers in a contest that highlighted the continuing power of Trump-aligned politics within the Republican Party.

sub.title: Trump’s Influence in the Primary
sub.descr: With Trump’s support, Biggs entered the primary as the front-runner, consolidating support among Republican voters in Arizona. His campaign was focused on conservative priorities such as border security, government spending and opposition to Democratic policies. It’s another win for Trump-backed candidates, who have managed to survive competitive Republican primaries in the 2026 election cycle.

sub.title: Arizona as a Key Battleground State
sub.descr: Arizona’s governor’s race is expected to be one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 election season. Arizona, a state that used to reliably vote Republican, has transformed into a competitive battleground with shifting demographics and voter coalitions, and its statewide elections have been closely divided, making it a key political target for both parties.

sub.title: Shaping Trump Influence in Republican Primary
sub.descr:
Former President Donald Trump’s dominance over GOP voters was on display in the Arizona Republican primary results. Biggs, a close ally of the Trump political movement, was buoyed by the strong support of conservative activists and voters who prioritized alignment with the former president’s agenda.

Biggs previously chaired the conservative House Freedom Caucus and developed a national reputation through his stances on immigration, government spending and election issues. His campaign emphasized his record as a conservative legislator and cast him as a candidate who could further Republican agendas at the state level.

sub.title: Challenges in the General Election
sub.descr:
His biggest victory came amid worries from some Republicans that candidates closely linked to Trump's movement might face challenges in general elections, particularly in places such as Arizona where independents frequently make the call in statewide races. Biggs’ critics said his conservative stances could energize the Republican base but also could make it harder to appeal to moderate voters.

The Republican primary also highlighted a wider rift in the party between candidates who push Trump-style populist conservatism and those who advocate a more traditional strategy aimed at broader electoral appeal.

sub.title: Arizona Governor’s Race Turns into National Political Battleground
sub.descr:
The race between Andy Biggs and Katie Hobbs for governor is expected to be one of the most competitive in the nation. Arizona has been playing a larger role in the political landscape of recent election cycles, with both parties spending heavily in the state because of its importance to national political power.

Democrats are expected to use Biggs’ conservative voting record and ties to Trump in their effort to keep the governor’s office. Hobbs’ campaign is expected to focus on issues like defending democratic institutions, protecting abortion access and keeping state government stable.

Republicans, meanwhile, see an opportunity to reclaim the governor’s mansion and bolster their standing in Arizona politics. GOP leaders say Biggs can appeal to voters worried about inflation, border security, housing costs and government spending.

sub.title: Broader Impact on Arizona Politics
sub.descr:
The key results in Arizona also changed the landscape in a number of congressional races outside the governor’s contest. The former president's influence with GOP voters was also reflected in another result: Trump-backed candidate Jay Feely won the Republican nomination for Arizona’s 1st Congressional District.

Arizona is likely to remain a prime target for national political groups, donors and campaign strategists with the general election approaching. Biggs-Hobbs’ November showdown will be a critical test of voter priorities and the trajectory of one of America’s most politically consequential swing states.

title: Senate Confirms Todd Blanche as Attorney General in Tight Overnight Vote
shortdescription: Todd Blanche, President Trump's former personal lawyer, was confirmed as attorney general by a razor-thin Senate margin after a bruising fight over a scrapped $1.8 billion settlement fund.

sub.title: A One-Vote Confirmation
sub.descr: In the early hours of Saturday morning, the Senate voted 50-49 to confirm Todd Blanche as the nation's next attorney general, handing President Donald Trump one of the narrowest Cabinet confirmation margins of his second term. Blanche, who had already been running the Justice Department in an acting role since the spring, will now take the job on a permanent footing — a shift that allies say will give him more room to push the administration's law enforcement priorities without the shadow of an unresolved nomination hanging over him. Two Republicans crossed the aisle to vote no, joining a unanimous bloc of Democrats in opposition, underscoring just how divisive the pick had become even within the president's own party.

sub.title: From Defense Attorney to Department Head
sub.descr: Blanche's path to the top of the Justice Department is unusual. He built his reputation not as a career prosecutor climbing the ranks, but as the defense lawyer who sat beside Trump during his New York hush money trial and represented him in two separate federal cases brought during the Biden administration. Blanche has repeatedly pointed to that experience as proof that he understands, firsthand, what he describes as the misuse of the justice system for political ends. He later joined the department as deputy attorney general before being elevated to acting head after Pam Bondi's firing this spring, meaning he has effectively been steering the agency for months already.

sub.title: The Settlement Fund That Nearly Sank Him
sub.descr: The nomination came close to collapsing over a controversial deal Blanche struck involving Trump's lawsuit against the IRS. As part of that settlement, the department floated a $1.8 billion fund intended to compensate people who claim they were mistreated by the criminal justice system, including some individuals tied to the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot. A related provision would have shielded Trump and his family from IRS audits. Several Republican senators balked, and the backlash threatened to stall his confirmation entirely. To keep his nomination alive, Blanche agreed in writing to abandon the compensation fund and scale back the audit protections — concessions that ultimately persuaded holdout senators like Bill Cassidy to back him.

sub.title: A Split Within the GOP
sub.descr: Even with the settlement walked back, the nomination didn't have smooth sailing. Senators Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska both broke from their party to vote against Blanche, with Murkowski arguing the department needs a leader willing to push back on the administration rather than simply carry out its wishes. Cassidy, who ended up casting a decisive supporting vote despite having lost his own primary to a Trump-aligned challenger this year, framed his support narrowly — describing it as a judgment about Blanche specifically rather than an endorsement of the president's broader agenda. Committee chairman Chuck Grassley was far more effusive, calling Blanche the right man for the job and pointing to his record running the department over the past several months.

sub.title: Democrats Warn of a Weaponized Department
sub.descr: Democrats used the floor debate to renew warnings that Blanche's closeness to Trump makes him unfit to lead an agency meant to operate independently of the White House. Senate Judiciary Committee ranking member Dick Durbin was among the most vocal critics, arguing that the moment called for an attorney general focused on rooting out corruption rather than settling political scores. Critics have pointed to the department's pursuit of Trump adversaries — including an indictment against former FBI Director James Comey that his legal team is now trying to get thrown out — as evidence of exactly the dynamic they fear. Blanche has also overseen a separate Florida-based inquiry, led by former Reagan-era prosecutor Joseph diGenova, examining whether past law enforcement and intelligence officials worked to undermine Trump, though it's unclear whether that investigation will produce any charges.

sub.title: What Comes Next
sub.descr: With confirmation behind him, Blanche now leads a department that has shed a significant share of its workforce over the past year through firings, resignations and departures under his and Bondi's tenure. Supporters argue his background as a courtroom lawyer — and the personal trust he's built with Trump — position him to push back on unreasonable demands from the White House more effectively than his predecessor could. Skeptics remain unconvinced, noting that Bondi was ousted after friction with judges, grand juries and career staff over efforts to build cases against the president's perceived enemies. Whether Blanche fares any differently in that balancing act is likely to shape how the department is viewed for the remainder of Trump's term.

title: Vote Republican or Risk Less Federal Help: How Trump Is Linking Aid to Midterm Outcomes
shortdescription: President Trump has repeatedly suggested on the campaign trail that states electing Democrats could see less federal assistance, weaving threats into rallies that also announce investments and policy breaks for Republican-led areas.

sub.title: A Recurring Campaign Theme Across Battlegrounds
sub.descr: President Donald Trump has turned a pointed message into a central theme of his midterm campaign stops this month. From Georgia to North Carolina, Kansas, and Ohio, he has repeatedly suggested that states electing Democrats could find his administration less eager to deliver federal assistance. The comments mix promises of investments and policy breaks for Republican-led areas with warnings about what might happen if voters choose the other side. Trump has sandwiched these remarks into rallies where he has also announced concrete benefits such as new semiconductor investments, a submarine repair center, and fewer limits on certain types of diesel fuel. The overall pitch underscores the kinds of tangible results an all-Republican Washington could continue to deliver if his party holds power after November. At the same time, the approach has drawn criticism for injecting politics into processes long treated as largely nonpolitical, including the distribution of disaster aid and benefits for veterans.

sub.title: Georgia: Collins Can Call Anytime, Ossoff Cannot
sub.descr: In Perry, Georgia, last week, Trump drew a sharp contrast between Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins and Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Collins, he said, could call whenever he wanted to ask for help for his state. If Georgia reelected Ossoff, it could be another story. Using a longtime derisive nickname, Trump referred to the senator as “Pee-wee Herman” and acted out a hypothetical phone call. If Ossoff asked for money for Georgia, Trump said he would respond that he did not care what the Democrat wanted. He later emphasized the difference between dealing with people he likes and those he does not, noting that personal relationships shape how presidents respond to requests. Trump acknowledged some might call the approach inappropriate, yet he presented it as simply human nature. “People don’t realize what a big difference it makes,” he told the crowd. Ossoff responded by calling it a losing strategy for a president he described as failed, one who insults and threatens voters while reminding them of higher costs under the current administration.

sub.title: North Carolina: Camp Lejeune Settlements Tied to Election Results
sub.descr: In North Carolina the strategy has drawn particular pushback. A 2022 law signed by then-President Joe Biden created a path for veterans and families affected by contaminated water at Camp Lejeune to seek compensation. At a Greenville rally earlier this month, Trump announced that roughly $1 billion in cash settlements had already been delivered and said he would direct the Justice Department to settle all remaining legitimate claims expeditiously — if Republicans won the House and Senate. “So, if we don’t win, there’s no money,” he said. “If we do win, you’re getting it.” Pressed later at the White House, Trump said another administration would have to handle the claims if Republicans lost, even though his own Justice Department currently manages the process. The remarks landed hard with some families. Jill Steen Dilgard, whose relatives served at Camp Lejeune and later developed serious illnesses, called the comments totally unacceptable. She described feeling physically sick and furious at the idea of conditioning care for military veterans on election results. “You’re playing politics and trying to bribe for a vote,” she said. “So many hundreds of thousands have already lost their lives, and hundreds of thousands are suffering.” Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper labeled the threats insulting and frustrating. His campaign has pressed Republican candidate Michael Whatley to denounce them. Whatley has said caring for the affected veterans and families remains a priority. Similar language appeared earlier in Gastonia, where Trump referenced remaining Hurricane Helene recovery money and said he would not send more if Whatley lost — before quickly adding that he was kidding.

sub.title: Kansas: Year-Round E15 Hinges on Marshall’s Reelection
sub.descr: In Kansas, Trump made an ethanol policy contingent on the Senate outcome while campaigning for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. He noted that his administration had already issued a temporary waiver allowing year-round sales of E15, the higher-ethanol fuel blend normally restricted in summer months. “With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent,” Trump said at a rally in Park City. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him.” Permanent year-round E15 can be achieved through legislation or continued administrative waivers issued by the Environmental Protection Agency. Hamilton’s campaign avoided direct criticism of Trump and instead said Kansans are tired of politics that treats public service like opposing teams. A spokesman noted that Marshall has not delivered permanent E15 in a decade in Congress and said Hamilton would look forward to working with anyone, including the president, to finally deliver on this and other important priorities for Kansas.

sub.title: Ohio: Personal Relationships Shape Federal Help
sub.descr: Ohio provided another example of the personal framing. In Vandalia, Trump observed that Republican officials had pressed him on disaster relief and that a president holds significant power over states. Referring to Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, he said he knew little about her, doubted she would call him, and predicted he would probably not work with her the same way. “I’m not gonna help her probably,” he added. Acton’s campaign responded that the candidate is committed to working with anyone, Democrat or Republican, to make life better for working Ohioans. The remarks fit a broader pattern in which Trump has suggested that liking the people who call him makes a practical difference in how federal resources are allocated.

sub.title: White House Defense and Democratic Pushback
sub.descr: White House officials have defended the broader approach. Spokesman Davis Ingle said Trump is committed to keeping a Republican majority in Congress so he can continue to deliver on what the administration calls a winning, common-sense agenda covering taxes, prescription drugs, immigration, and other priorities. Democrats, the White House argued, have made it clear they have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people. Opponents see a different picture. Critics argue the remarks turn public resources into political leverage and undermine the expectation that disaster aid, veterans’ benefits, and other federal help should not depend on which party controls a state’s congressional seats. The strategy sits within a larger effort to make the midterms personal to Trump and to energize his base by pairing tangible announcements with warnings about reduced help under Democratic wins.

sub.title: What the Approach Means for the Midterms
sub.descr: Across these stops the same dynamic repeats: promises of investment and relief for places that deliver Republican victories, coupled with suggestions that Democratic successes could slow or stop the flow of help. Supporters hear a president fighting for his agenda and his allies. Critics hear an improper mixing of politics with the basic obligations of government. Whether the approach ultimately helps or hurts Republican candidates remains to be tested at the ballot box. What is already clear is that traditional norms around the even-handed delivery of federal aid and benefits have become part of the partisan contest this cycle. With the midterms approaching, both sides are using the remarks to define the choice before voters and to frame the stakes of control of Congress.

author.name: Sarah Mitchell
author.bio: Sarah Mitchell has covered Capitol Hill and state-level politics for over a decade, with a focus on voting rights, redistricting, and election law. Her reporting has appeared in outlets across the country, and she is based in Nashville.
